# Master register — every open item, and what closes it

**Generated by `npm run master` from the five sources declared in
[`OUTSTANDING_SOURCES.json`](./OUTSTANDING_SOURCES.json).**
Do not edit by hand — `npm run test:master` fails on drift.

> **58 items are open** across 5 sources.
> 31 state what would decisively close them; **27 do not**.
> 41 name someone who can act; 17 do not.
> 22 are sequence-dependent,
> 5 independent, and
> 31 carry no stated ordering relation at all.

[`OUTSTANDING.md`](./OUTSTANDING.md) answers *how much is left*. This answers *what each one is
and what would close it*. [`CLOSED.md`](./CLOSED.md) is the counterpart for the 58
items already discharged.

---

## How to read this

Every column is either **read from the item's source** or **derived from ordering relations the
sources state**. Nothing is filled in with a plausible sentence, and the distinction is the point
of the document.

| Column | Where it comes from |
|---|---|
| What it is | The source's own description. |
| Why it is | The source's own statement of why it exists or why it is still open. |
| Current state | The source's status, or — for the three sources with no status convention — the position their own preamble states for every entry. |
| Actions, steps, inputs | The source's steps, requirements, decisions and constraints. |
| What decisively closes it | The source's resolution criterion. **27 of 58 items have none**, and are marked *not established by the source* with what would establish one. |
| Execution topology | Derived. See below. |

### The three topologies

| Verdict | Count | What it means |
|---|---:|---|
| `SEQUENCE-DEPENDENT` | 22 | Its own source names something that must come first, or names it as something that must come first for another item, or states a sentence that constrains the order. Position in the sequence is not free. |
| `INDEPENDENT` | 5 | Its source names prerequisites and every one of them has closed. It is released: it can start now, in any order relative to the rest, and nothing open is waiting on it. |
| `PARALLEL-EXECUTION-NEUTRAL` | 31 | No source states any ordering relation involving this item, in either direction. Read this as *the record constrains nothing* — not as proof that running it alongside anything else is safe. An absence of a stated dependency is not a demonstration of independence, and four of the five sources state dependencies for no item at all. |

**The derivation is stated, not asserted.** Each item below carries the sentence its verdict rests
on — the prerequisite it waits for, the item that waits for it, or the ordering sentence its source
writes. Where the verdict is `PARALLEL-EXECUTION-NEUTRAL` the basis reads *no source states an
ordering relation involving it*, which is a statement about the record and not about the work.
Only two of the five sources state dependencies for any item; the other three state none for any,
so their entries land in that bucket by silence rather than by analysis. Treat it as *unconstrained
by the record* and verify before running two of them together.

## Lens 4 · Commissioning versus production readiness

14 of the 58 open items stand between this estate and a commissioned
endpoint surface. The rest are real work that does not gate it — governance features, notification
carriers, audit findings against a package that is not in the commissioning path.

The governance half is read, not judged: the position file carries `blocksCommissioning` on every
finding. **The readiness half is a judgement made here** — the register carries a category, and
this document treats `BLOCKING`, `MANUAL_GATE`, `PROVISIONING` and `APPLY` as gating and
`CORRECTNESS`, `DEBT`, `ARCHITECTURE` and `UNSPECIFIED` as not. That mapping is a choice, it is
stated here so it can be disagreed with, and it is the one line in this document that is neither
read from a source nor derived from one.

## Lens 5 · By whether anything states how to close it

The single largest gap in this estate's bookkeeping, and it is structural rather than careless.
Two sources of five state a closure criterion per item — the readiness register, which carries
`resolutionCriteria` on all 22, and the governance position, whose 9 close on a condition
`npm run test:closure` already enforces. The other three state none for any of their 56, and 43
of those state no action either: what is written down is the finding, not the remedy.

## Every open item, in full

### ITEM-2

**The tenant write path has never been executed**

`BLOCKING` · source: [Production readiness register](../../docs/deployment/PRODUCTION_READINESS_REGISTER.json) · actor: operator

**What it is.** scripts/update-flow-definition.ps1 PATCHes a flow definition back to the tenant, which is the same call the designer makes on Save. It has never been run. The patch track is no longer the only delivery route: PowerShell was dropped from the automation on 2026-09-08 because PnP.PowerShell needs an Entra app registration the estate had already ruled out, and the paste track — docs/deployment/internal/flows/console-apply/, one snippet per flow package, generated by npm run console:apply — needs no PowerShell, no app registration and no tenant admin. What is still unproven is that ANY write reaches the tenant from outside the designer, which is what this item is for; prove it by whichever route you intend to deliver by.

**Why it is.** Requires tenant credentials and a Power Automate session. Nothing in this repository can execute it. (Criterion corrected 2026-09-15. It previously read "The dry run prints the flow name and action count without error" — which this item's own steps contradicted, since step 2 asks for a fresh export carrying the change. The steps were right and the criterion was wrong: a dry run does not write, and the title of this item is that the WRITE path has never been executed. Ten items name ITEM-2 as a prerequisite and every one of them needs its endpoint exercised, which a rehearsal cannot deliver. Closing this on a dry run would have been the applied-versus-observed collapse this register exists to prevent, committed on the item that gates the most.)

**Current state.** BLOCKED · no target date established

**Actions, steps and inputs required.**

1. Apply one flow by the route you intend to use. Console route: open make.powerautomate.com, open any flow you own so the page holds a token, then paste one file from docs/deployment/internal/flows/console-apply/ into the browser devtools console — it carries DRY_RUN = true and changes nothing on the first paste. PowerShell route: the dry run documented in docs/deployment/sharepoint/remediation/patched/README.md. (Corrected 2026-09-15: this step cited remediation/patched/README.md, a path that does not exist in this repository — the file is under docs/deployment/sharepoint/. The evidence entry on this item already carried the full path; only the step text was wrong, so an operator following the step hit a dead end while the citation beside it resolved.)
2. Confirm it reports the flow name and action count, and that a fresh export carries the change.
3. Record the result; if it fails, raise it before any delivery-track item proceeds.

_Inputs that must be supplied:_

- The dry run must be used first; it sends nothing.

**What decisively closes it.** One flow carries a change that was applied from outside the Power Automate designer, and a fresh export of that flow contains it. The dry run is the mandatory first pass and is not on its own sufficient: it reads and reports, and this item exists to prove that a WRITE reaches the tenant.

**How closure would be checked.** Two artefacts, recorded against the flow they were taken on: the dry-run console output, and a fresh export of the same flow showing the applied change. Without the second, nothing distinguishes a reachable API from a successful write.

**Execution topology.** `SEQUENCE-DEPENDENT` — G-04, ITEM-6, ITEM-11, ITEM-12, ITEM-56 name it as a prerequisite. [`G-04`](#g-04), [`ITEM-6`](#item-6), [`ITEM-11`](#item-11), [`ITEM-12`](#item-12), [`ITEM-56`](#item-56) wait on it.

### G-04

**No server-side enforcement is running anywhere**

`BLOCKING` · source: [Production readiness register](../../docs/deployment/PRODUCTION_READINESS_REGISTER.json) · actor: Power Automate (implementation); agency (posture decision)

**What it is.** The authenticating proxy that would have validated tokens, derived roles and authorised actions was built and then removed rather than deployed. Every obligation it carried now belongs to each flow individually: token validation, role derivation, per-action authorisation, rate limiting, reference minting, upload ticketing and the filename policy. Caller identity is a client-asserted userEmail read from localStorage.

**Why it is.** The work is in Power Automate, not in this repository. No code here can close it.

**Current state.** BLOCKED · no target date established

**Actions, steps and inputs required.**

1. Decide the posture (pilot vs enforced) — agency.
2. If enforced: implement token validation, role derivation and per-action authorisation in each flow.
3. Set auth.enabled and supply tenant configuration.
4. Verify a viewer cannot reach a privileged action by editing local storage.

_Inputs that must be supplied:_

- Whether to go live in the pilot posture, or hold until enforcement runs. This is an agency risk decision, not a technical one.
- The generated packages already carry rate limiting, reference minting and upload ticketing. Token validation, role derivation and per-action authorisation are not in them.

**What decisively closes it.** A flow called directly with a forged or absent identity refuses the action.

**How closure would be checked.** A direct call to each endpoint bypassing the client, asserting refusal. npm run commission ceases to report the pilot-posture warning.

**Execution topology.** `SEQUENCE-DEPENDENT` — waits on ITEM-2 — still open. Waits on [`ITEM-2`](#item-2).

### ITEM-44

**The client spoke a protocol neither OTP flow reads — reconciled on the client side**

`BLOCKING` · source: [Production readiness register](../../docs/deployment/PRODUCTION_READINESS_REGISTER.json) · actor: operator (the live proof); the direction is settled

**What it is.** core/data-client.js sends action "otpGenerate"/"otpVerify" from config/endpoints.config.js and nests everything under payload; both OTP flows switch on action "generate"/"verify" and read identifier and otp_code at the top level. Neither the dispatch value nor the field placement matches, so the Switch matches no case and neither OTP path runs. This is not caused by the ITEM-43 cutover — the old flow has the same case values — and is consistent with ITEM-2: nothing has ever exercised it. It fails loudly: varStatusCode starts at 500 and the Response returns it, so an unmatched request answers 500 rather than a misleading 200. Two further findings sit alongside it: Case_Generate mails the code to the literal dgsregistry@nitda.gov.ng rather than to the requester, and writes item/Title from identifier with no coalesce while the verify lookup binds on Title through a four-way one — so a caller sending userEmail writes an empty Title that verify can never match.

**Why it is.** The direction is decided and implemented, and the seam is now asserted on every build. What is NOT done is the only thing that can settle it: no request has ever been made. This item stays open until one is, because a protocol that reads correctly and has never been exercised is exactly what produced the defect.

**Current state.** APPLIED_UNVERIFIED · none established; no item in this register carries a target date

**Actions, steps and inputs required.**

1. Done — the client sends action generate/verify with identifier and otp_code at the top level.
2. Done — npm run test:otpprotocol asserts the seam against the deployed definitions.
3. Outstanding — the recipient decision: Case_Generate mails the code to the literal dgsregistry@nitda.gov.ng rather than to the requester. That is a flow change and an agency call.
4. Outstanding — run the four cutover tests through the platform (ITEM-43).

_Inputs that must be supplied:_

- DIRECTION SETTLED 2026-09-04: reconcile on the CLIENT, not the flows. The two flows already agree with each other — Web - OTP Generate and IP_OTP_VERIFY both read identifier and otp_code at the top level and switch on generate/verify — so the client was the single outlier and one change fixes both. Changing the flows instead would mean a second designer paste into a flow certified hours earlier, plus a change to a second flow nobody has reviewed, to reach the same place.
- The mechanism is the client's own: flatPayload already existed for flows that read their fields where they were sent, and modules/single-assignment.js already uses it. No new mechanism was introduced.
- Blast radius is nil: each endpoint's action is an independent frozen entry and flatPayload is per-call, so no other endpoint's wire format changed. The options passthrough added to invokeObsidianAction is additive — every existing caller passes two arguments and gets {}.
- The estate has two conventions and both are correct: the portal posts flat bodies with no action because one flow serves one endpoint; the internal runtime dispatches {action, payload} because DYNAMIC_ACTIONS and EMAIL share a flow. The OTP flows are switch-dispatched, so they need an action — the disagreement was vocabulary, not architecture.

**What decisively closes it.** One request from the platform reaches a matched Switch case, and one code issued through the platform verifies through the platform. Until both are observed against the tenant, this is unresolved regardless of what the code reads like.

**How closure would be checked.** Read from the tenant, not from the repository: a run history entry on IP_OTP_VERIFY showing Case_Verify entered, and an OTP_Transactions row whose Title equals the identity the platform sent.

**Execution topology.** `PARALLEL-EXECUTION-NEUTRAL` — no source states an ordering relation involving it, in either direction.

### ITEM-51

**Officers are never told of assignments, approvals, escalations, delegations or reminders**

`CORRECTNESS` · source: [Production readiness register](../../docs/deployment/PRODUCTION_READINESS_REGISTER.json) · actor: Platform technical owner, with the correspondence lifecycle process owner for the copy-to decision

**What it is.** The assignment cascade requires an assignee and a due date on every assignment and resolves a supporting unit, a supporting assignee and a copy-to list besides. Neither DGO_SINGLE_ASSIGNMENT nor DGO_BULK_ASSIGNMENT carries any mail action, so none of those audiences is written to. pending_review can only be left by a second person's decision and nothing tells that person it is waiting. The acknowledgment module's remind-assignee and FastTrack's notify-owner both report to the operator that a notice was queued; both write only to browser storage, and notify-owner has no action-ownership spec at all, so it runs with no declared backend or audit vocabulary. The FastTrack escalation action writes an escalation record with status Open that reaches nobody, escalate-non-ack is a charter capability with no implementation at all, the orchestrator's set-reminder records a dueAt that nothing reads at that time, and executive-escalate delegates a record to a person who is never told it is theirs. Separately, Deployed - Create Task DOES notify the assignee from the task's AssignedTo field — and DGO_SINGLE_ASSIGNMENT, the package that replaces it, carries no mail action, so pasting it removes the one working assignment notice in the estate.

**Why it is.** Two clocks start on every assignment and the person they run against is not told they have started. The two actions that claim to notify someone are the more serious half: an operator who reads 'Owner notification queued' has been told a message is on its way, and nothing is queued anywhere but that browser.

- Change remind-assignee's backend from DYNAMIC_ACTIONS.optional to mandatory, or change the operator copy so it does not claim the assignee was reminded.

- Re-run npm run notifications -- --check and npm run test:governance.

- RN-020 is in-app only and is bounded by the notification centre being device-local by design.

### GOV-04

**None of the four HTTP governance endpoints returns an outcome to its caller**

`contract` · source: [Governance estate position](../../docs/reference/governance-estate-position.json) · actor: Platform technical owner

**What it is.** 02, 03 and 07 declare no Response action at all. 05 declares one — `Reply` — but it runs after `Scope_05_GOV_Retire_HTTP_Flow_COMPLETE_UPDATED`, and every path through that scope ends in a Terminate, so `Reply` is unreachable. In all four cases the caller receives Power Automate's default acknowledgement and never learns what happened. Worse, the validation failures terminate with runStatus Failed AFTER the trigger has already accepted the request, so a caller that submits an invalid registration, an unrecorded execution, or a retirement of a flow that is not in the registry sees the same acknowledgement as one that succeeded.

**Why it is.** A registering system cannot tell registration from rejection, so the registry silently under-records and the ledger silently drops executions. This is the same failure the portal's V-02 finding fixed on the citizen side: reporting acceptance for something that was not accepted.

**Current state.** repository: CORRECTED DEFINITIONS PRODUCED. docs/deployment/governance/flows/*.corrected.json add a reachable Response before every Terminate on all four flows — 15 responses in total. Reachability, status/runStatus agreement and body determinism are asserted by tests/governance-flow-corrections.test.mjs. · tenant: OUTSTANDING. The deployed flows are unchanged until GOVERNANCE-TENANT-RUNBOOK.md Step 4 is applied.

**Actions, steps and inputs required.**

- Give each of the four a Response action on every path — success and each Terminate branch — carrying the estate's response envelope, and place it before the Terminate rather than after the scope. For 05, move `Reply` inside the scope ahead of the terminations, or drop it: unreachable code that looks like a reply is worse than none.

**What decisively closes it.** Give each of the four a Response action on every path — success and each Terminate branch — carrying the estate's response envelope, and place it before the Terminate rather than after the scope. For 05, move `Reply` inside the scope ahead of the terminations, or drop it: unreachable code that looks like a reply is worse than none. — then moved to closedFindings with repositoryStatus and tenantStatus both reading resolved, which npm run test:closure enforces.

**How closure would be checked.** npm run test:governanceestate · npm run test:closure

### GOV-05

**The retirement endpoint cascades unconditionally, and anyone holding its URL can call it**

`high` · source: [Governance estate position](../../docs/reference/governance-estate-position.json) · actor: Platform technical owner, with the governance owner for the approval decision

**What it is.** 05 - GOV - Retire HTTP Flow accepts an anonymous POST of {environmentId, flowId, retirementReason} — triggerAuthenticationType All, so the SAS signature in the URL is the whole of the authentication. It then retires the registry row, closes every current contract version, and marks every non-retired consumer and every non-retired dependency as Retired, before resolving the flow's open exceptions. The workbook's own key control for this scenario reads: 'verify no active consumers/dependencies remain' and 'stop new traffic before technical removal'. The flow does not verify. It retires them, which erases the evidence that any were active.

**Why it is.** One request removes a flow's governance record and every relationship recorded against it, and — per GOV-04 — returns no body saying what it removed. There is no approval step, no dry run, and no way for the caller to discover the blast radius before or after.

**Current state.** repository: CORRECTED DEFINITION PRODUCED. The cascade is gated by If_Safe_To_Retire: both active counts are taken before any write, retirement is blocked with 409 when either is non-zero, and proceeds only when both are zero or force is true. Retire_Registry was lifted out of If_Registry_Found, where it would otherwise have escaped the guard — a defect the test found, not the design. A forced retirement is recorded with both counts. · tenant: OUTSTANDING. GOVERNANCE-TENANT-RUNBOOK.md Step 4.3 validates all four paths against the live flow.

**Actions, steps and inputs required.**

- Implement the documented control: count active consumers and dependencies first and refuse the retirement when any exist, returning them to the caller so the owner can act. Keep the cascade behind an explicit force flag that is recorded on the registry row. Consider whether an operation this destructive should be anonymous at all — Tenant authentication is available and is what IP_SCAN_INTAKE already uses.

**What decisively closes it.** Implement the documented control: count active consumers and dependencies first and refuse the retirement when any exist, returning them to the caller so the owner can act. Keep the cascade behind an explicit force flag that is recorded on the registry row. Consider whether an operation this destructive should be anonymous at all — Tenant authentication is available and is what IP_SCAN_INTAKE already uses. — then moved to closedFindings with repositoryStatus and tenantStatus both reading resolved, which npm run test:closure enforces.

**How closure would be checked.** npm run test:governanceestate · npm run test:closure

**Execution topology.** `SEQUENCE-DEPENDENT` — the source states a constraint against a condition rather than another item: "It does not block the endpoint commissioning path, and it is not live until the seven registry lists are provisioned.".

### GOV-06

**The exported flow definitions and the tenant register cannot be joined**

`measurement` · source: [Governance estate position](../../docs/reference/governance-estate-position.json) · actor: Platform technical owner

**What it is.** The repository holds 77 exported flow definitions, each identified by a 36-character Power Automate flow GUID. The register holds 51 workflow records, each identified by a 32-hex Logic Apps workflow id. These are different identifier spaces for the same objects, and ZERO exported definitions carry an id the register knows. Joining on normalised display name — the only field the two share — matches 13. That leaves 64 exported definitions the register does not name and 37 register workflows for which no definition is held, with 1 name reused across records.

**Why it is.** Nobody can answer 'is this exported flow one of the 51?' — so any statement comparing the two counts is comparing populations measured on different axes. This audit made that mistake: an earlier recommendation set '77 exported definitions' against '51 tenant workflows' as though one contained the other. It does not, and the overlap is 13.

**Current state.** repository: BLOCKERS 1 AND 2 CLOSED, 2026-09-10. WorkflowId is in the registry specification (scripts/lib/registry-spec-amendments.mjs, applied by the extractor so the JSON stays derived), and flow 02 accepts `workflowId` on its trigger, refuses a dashed 36-character flowId with 400, and writes the value on both arms of the registry upsert. Blockers 3 and 4 are not defects and cannot be closed: only 56 of 77 exported definitions carry an HTTP trigger, and idOverlap is ceilinged at 51. scripts/reconcile-flow-definitions.mjs still maintains the name-based map and states its limits. · tenant: OUTSTANDING. Nothing has been provisioned or applied. Step 5.3a creates the column; Step 4 applies the corrected flow 02; Step 6 populates the join. NOTE: flow 01's Compose_Final_Report_JSON.validation.expectedFields and the configuration seed ProvisioningSchemaExpectedFieldCount both still state 101. Provisioning 102 columns without updating them makes flow 01 report a variance against a correct run.

**Actions, steps and inputs required.**

- Record both identifiers in one place. DGO_HTTPFlowRegistry is designed to do exactly this — FlowId alongside RegistryKey, written once at registration — which is the strongest single argument for adopting it. Until then, npm run reconcile:definitions maintains the name-based map and states its own limits, and tests/governance-estate.test.mjs holds the numbers so the gap cannot be quoted wrongly again.

**What decisively closes it.** Record both identifiers in one place. DGO_HTTPFlowRegistry is designed to do exactly this — FlowId alongside RegistryKey, written once at registration — which is the strongest single argument for adopting it. Until then, npm run reconcile:definitions maintains the name-based map and states its own limits, and tests/governance-estate.test.mjs holds the numbers so the gap cannot be quoted wrongly again. — then moved to closedFindings with repositoryStatus and tenantStatus both reading resolved, which npm run test:closure enforces.

**A live producer wrote seed rows to the NON-authoritative site thirteen days after the audit**

`data-integrity` · source: [Governance estate position](../../docs/reference/governance-estate-position.json) · actor: Platform technical owner, with the governance owner for the flow correction

**What it is.** The Step 3 survey of 2026-09-09 read all 17 duplicate list instances on NITDADGO-EAAACTIVITYTRACKING. Thirteen are empty. Four carry items: DGO_AuditLog 5, DGO_RoleCatalogue 6, DGO_UserDirectory 1, DGO_PilotCohorts 1. All four report LastItemModifiedDate 2026-08-31T01:58:48-49Z — within one second of each other, which is one run, not four accidents. The list capture this estate reasons from is dated 2026-08-18, so the write happened THIRTEEN DAYS AFTER the audit that recorded these lists as duplicates to retire.

**Why it is.** Step 3's delete phase cannot be executed until the producer is known. Deleting a list nothing writes to is housekeeping; deleting a list something still writes to breaks that producer silently.

**Current state.** repository: MEASURED AND TOOLED. scripts/build-governance-comparison.mjs emits a read-only row-by-row comparison of every duplicate against the instance that supersedes it, keyed on the list's own seed key field rather than Title — two of these lists legitimately repeat titles. Nine duplicates declare no key field; all nine are empty, and the script reports CANNOT COMPARE rather than guessing at row identity. · tenant: SURVEY, EXPORT AND RENAME COMPLETE, 2026-09-09. All 17 duplicates exported (13 items in total: DGO_AuditLog 5, DGO_RoleCatalogue 6, DGO_UserDirectory 1, DGO_PilotCohorts 1; 0 failed) and all 17 renamed to ZZ_RETIRED_* (0 failed). The rename has already had its intended effect on one known hazard: every deployed reference to these lists is by title, so ZZ_RETIRED_ makes those calls 404 rather than silently hit a duplicate. DELETE remains blocked until the producer of the 2026-08-31 rows is identified in the tenant.

**Actions, steps and inputs required.**

- Two things, in order. First, scripts/compare-duplicate-governance-lists.browser.js answers whether any row exists ONLY in a duplicate — if one does, it is the sole copy and must be reconciled before any deletion. Second, find and correct the producer, which is Step 4 work: nothing readable from a list says what wrote to it. Only then does Step 3's delete phase become safe. Step 3's survey, export and rename phases are unaffected and should proceed — the rename is precisely what makes a live producer fail loudly while the fix is still one restore away.

### GOV-11

**A parallel flow-truth database was provisioned outside the specification, by title, on an unrecorded site, without the internal-name hint**

`data-integrity` · source: [Governance estate position](../../docs/reference/governance-estate-position.json) · actor: Platform technical owner

**What it is.** Two browser scripts — NITDA_Flow_Truth_SharePoint_Provisioning_BROWSER_CONSOLE1.js and NITDA_Flow_Truth_SharePoint_Provisioning_RESUME_FIX.js — were reported executed against the tenant on 2026-09-10. Between them they create two lists and one document library titled 'NITDA Flow Truth Registry', 'NITDA Flow Truth History' and 'NITDA Flow Truth Artefacts', with 37, 37 and 16 columns respectively (90 column creations), five views, three folders, and uniqueness enforced on RegistryKey and HistoryKey. None of the three appears in docs/reference/http-flow-registry-spec.json, sharepoint-provisioning-spec.json, portal-field-spec.json, internal-field-evidence.json, or the 326-list capture of 2026-08-18.

**Why it is.** The estate now has, or may have, a second implementation of the flow-truth database beside the one it specifies: 3 resources and 90 columns provisioned ad hoc, against 7 lists and 101 fields specified and guarded. Two implementations of one capability is the condition GOV-02 describes at list level — a writer populating one while a reader queries the other, both succeeding, neither seeing the other. Because the site was never pinned or recorded, the repository cannot say which site received it, so it cannot say whether GOV-01's authoritative site now carries unspecified lists or whether the non-authoritative site does. B1 of the flow-truth review is measured against the 2026-08-18 capture and is therefore no longer a statement about the live tenant.

**Current state.** repository: MEASURED against the scripts themselves. Every claim above is read from the two files; none is read from the tenant. · tenant: UNMEASURED. Execution is reported, not observed. Whether the resources exist, on which site, and under which internal names is unknown until scripts/verify-flow-truth-provisioning.browser.js is run.

**Actions, steps and inputs required.**

- Do not run either script again — a re-run is the duplication case, not a repair. Run the read-only scripts/verify-flow-truth-provisioning.browser.js on BOTH sites to establish what exists, on which site, under which internal names, and how many disambiguated copies. Only then decide between adopting the three resources into http-flow-registry-spec.json and retiring them in favour of the specified seven lists. Both are agency decisions; neither is the executing agent's to make.

**What decisively closes it.** Do not run either script again — a re-run is the duplication case, not a repair. ## What this register does not do

**It does not prioritise.** Items are not equal: one agency decision can gate ten provisioning
steps, and the flow-truth review's 0 findings are all against a
single package that is not in the commissioning path. Read
[`ACTION_PLAN.md`](./ACTION_PLAN.md) for order of work.

**It does not close anything.** Status lives in the five sources. An item leaves this document when
its source says it has closed — and `npm run test:closure` holds every document, and
`npm run commission` itself, to that.

**It cannot tell you a finding in a record has been overtaken.** Audits are never edited to agree
with the present, so their findings stay counted until an item in a tracked source supersedes them
by id. That is the honest default and occasionally an overcount.

**Where this document and a command disagree, the command governs.**

```bash
npm run master        # regenerate this document
npm run outstanding   # the total: 58 open across 5 sources
npm run closed        # the 58 already discharged
npm run readiness     # the register of record's own tally
npm run commission    # what a commissioning run reports today
```
